summary: Defines a URL scheme for pointing at things on an IMAP mail server, such as a mailbox or a single message. This lets links to mail, and the details needed to log in and fetch it, be written down in a standard form. It is a proposed standard and was replaced by RFC 5092.

eli5.summary: It is like a street address for an email folder or one letter inside it, so a program knows exactly where to go and what to pick up.

questions: how to link to an email message on an imap server
what does auth=* mean in an imap url
subtitle: A standard way to write a link to an IMAP server, a mailbox, a search result, a message or one part of a message.

tldr.problem: IMAP gives access to remote message stores, but there was no standard way to write down a reference to an IMAP server, mailbox or message the way a web link refers to a page.
tldr.mechanism: The imap: URL scheme has four forms, for a server, a list of mailboxes, a set of messages and a single message or message part. Each form maps to a fixed set of IMAP commands, and an optional user name and authentication mechanism say how to log in.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from September 1997 and was replaced by RFC 5092.

facts.label: Anonymous login
facts.value: user name anonymous, e-mail address as password

today: RFC 2192 is a Proposed Standard from September 1997 that was obsoleted by RFC 5092, which is the one to read for the current definition of IMAP URLs.

sections.title: The IMAP URL Scheme
sections.content:
IMAP is a rich protocol for accessing remote message stores, which makes it a good fit for public mailing list archives as well as private and shared mail. This RFC defines a URL scheme for referencing objects on an IMAP server: servers, mailboxes, messages, MIME bodies and search programs.

An IMAP URL follows the common Internet scheme syntax of RFC 1738, with one exception: clear text passwords are not permitted. If no port is given, it defaults to 143.
sections.eli5: A web link points to a web page. This gives email folders and messages their own kind of link.

sections.title: The Four URL Forms
sections.content:
An IMAP URL takes one of four forms, and each one tells the program which IMAP commands to run.

  • Server, imap://<iserver>/: show the contents of the server. This is likely equivalent to a mailbox list of type LIST or LSUB, and the program SHOULD use LSUB if it supports subscriptions.
  • List of mailboxes: the URL ends with ;TYPE=LIST or ;TYPE=LSUB, which MUST be included. If the mailbox part is omitted, the program SHOULD use a percent sign if it supports a hierarchical view and an asterisk otherwise.
  • List of messages: the mailbox name is used with the IMAP SELECT command. An optional ? part is used as the arguments of an IMAP SEARCH command.
  • Message or part: a /;UID= value is used with UID FETCH. An optional /;SECTION= value picks one part, and without it the URL refers to the entire message.

A mailbox or message URL may carry ;UIDVALIDITY=, the value from the IMAP UIDVALIDITY response when the URL was created. A program SHOULD use it to detect that the URL is stale. Unsafe or reserved characters MUST be encoded as RFC 1738 describes, but a / in a mailbox name SHOULD NOT be encoded.
sections.eli5: The address can point at the whole post office, at one shelf of folders, at a pile of letters that match a search, or at one single letter or one page inside it.

sections.title: User Names and Authentication
sections.content:
A URL may carry a user name and an authentication mechanism, added to the end of the user name as ;AUTH=<type>. They are used with the IMAP LOGIN or AUTHENTICATE commands. With no user name or mechanism, the program logs in as anonymous and uses the end user's Internet e-mail address as the password. A user name with no mechanism is treated as ;AUTH=*.

;AUTH=* means the client SHOULD pick a suitable mechanism, from those listed by the CAPABILITY command or from an out of band service that gives a PREAUTH connection. If none fits and no user name was given, it SHOULD fall back to anonymous login. That lets one URL give read-write access to authorized users and read-only anonymous access to everyone else.

Because URLs can come from untrusted sources, a program that resolves a URL needing credentials must meet at least one of five criteria. Examples are that the URL comes from a trusted source, that local site policy allows the server, that the user confirms, or that the mechanism validates the server first. A program MAY reuse open connections, but only ones authenticated as the same user, or anonymous ones if the URL names no user.
sections.eli5: The link can say who you are and how to prove it. If it says nothing, you walk in as a guest, and a careful program checks that the door is the right one before handing over your key.

sections.title: Relative URLs and Mailbox Names
sections.content:
Relative IMAP URLs are allowed and are resolved by the rules of RFC 1808, except that parameters are treated as part of the normal path. The authentication part counts as part of the user name, so a relative URL inherits the mechanism of its base URL unless it names a new login or server. URLs always use / as the hierarchy delimiter, but IMAP lets mailboxes use any delimiter. Relative mailbox paths therefore work only when the mailbox uses /; otherwise the whole name must be given or inherited as a whole.

For a message or part, the base URL comes from the Content-Base or Content-Location headers of the MIME entity and its enclosing entities, as defined for HTTP.

IMAP encodes non-US-ASCII mailbox names in a private convention called modified UTF-7. For URLs, that MUST be converted to UTF-8, and the 8-bit characters are then percent-encoded. Appendix A gives sample C code for the conversion.
sections.eli5: A short link can borrow the front part of a longer one, like saying 'next door' instead of the whole address. Folder names in other alphabets are translated into a form that fits inside a link.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Section 10 shows how a client might turn URLs into IMAP commands. An anonymous URL for message UID 20 in the mailbox gray-council leads to an anonymous LOGIN, a SELECT, a check that UIDVALIDITY matches, and then UID FETCH 20 BODY.PEEK[].

A URL with ;AUTH=KERBEROS_V4 leads to an AUTHENTICATE command instead of LOGIN, and a /;section=1.2 suffix leads to BODY.PEEK[1.2]. In the last example, ;AUTH=* lets the client read the server's CAPABILITY list and pick a mechanism, and a query turns into a SEARCH. The RFC notes the client has implementation dependent choices there.
sections.eli5: The examples show the steps a mail program takes after you click one of these links: knock, say who you are, open the folder, and fetch the letter.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of the IMAP specification and of the URL specification apply, as do the authenticated-URL cautions in the authentication section. Many email clients store the plain text password for later use. Such clients MUST NOT use a stored password in response to an IMAP URL without explicit permission from the user to supply that password to the specified host name.

URLs without a user name, and URLs containing ;AUTH=*, need extra care, since they are more likely to expose the user's primary account or to fall back on a weaker mechanism. Clients are discouraged from falling back to a plain text password with ;AUTH=* unless the connection has strong encryption.
sections.eli5: A link could secretly lead to a fake mail server. So a mail program must ask you before it hands your saved password to a place it does not know.

data.title: Anonymous fetch of one message
data.code:
<imap://minbari.org/gray-council;UIDVALIDITY=385759045/;UID=20>

<connect to minbari.org, port 143>
C: A001 LOGIN ANONYMOUS sheridan@babylon5.org
C: A002 SELECT gray-council
<client verifies the UIDVALIDITY matches>
C: A003 UID FETCH 20 BODY.PEEK[]
